orsolya_vance.name: Lamp-Mother Orsolya Vance
orsolya_vance.personality: broad, weathered, fierce in a motherly way; every sentence sounds like an instruction to eat something
orsolya_vance.voice: wick, wax and oil measured out like a litany; counts the village's lamps as other people count prayers

say: Orsolya Vance, Lamp-Mother of the Hold. Warm yourself. Eat first, talk second. A hungry traveller makes the poorest listener.

Four hundred and twelve lamps burn in this village, and none has gone out in a hundred years. We keep them because the moor is not kind in the dark. Two months ago a new light appeared on the stone-ring hill, a pale one, and the moor changed. Wolves that slumbered through generations woke up, and walked on two legs.

The lord of the moor, Garrow Thane, wears the pale lamp's leash now. He sits at the ring, and he is hungry for something no hunter can feed. Go up through the depths and put out that lamp. Take silver oil from Tobias: ghosts do not mind a plain blade, and wolves of the night mind silver very much.
The moon came out. I stood on the Hold's wall and watched it come, thin and white, and I put down my snuffer and wept. Four hundred and twelve lamps, and none of them as good as that one moon.
Garrow is alive? Then he will be fed, and clothed, and given a bed by my own hearth. A man who endured thirty years under a bad light deserves some honest warmth.

Here is a purse from the Hold's common fund, and a lamp of your own. Keep Vael lies west, up the black cliffs, and here is the pass-token for the chain. Walk it carefully. And remember what the moor taught us: a single flame, tended, is a very large thing.

lines.text: A lamp is a small promise to the dark: here, a little longer. Break enough small promises and the dark stops listening.
I trim each wick with my own scissors. They were my grandmother's. They have cut four hundred thousand wicks, and none has ever been wasted.
The moor was never friendly, but it was never hungry. That changed on the night the pale lamp was lit.
Oil is life in the Hold. We press it from moor-poppy seed, we filter it twice, and we spend it as if each drop were a day.
Children here learn to light a lamp before they learn to read. The two arts have a great deal in common.
If a lamp dies at night, someone must relight it before the next breath. That is the rule. We have broken it once, and we do not discuss the year.
Sword-bearer, steel alone will not trouble the wraiths of the moor. They drift through it like smoke. Silver, fire or a spell, though, and they scream.
Caster, you will be this moor's friend. Wraiths cannot ward against a spell, and the wolves fear light above all else.
Light-foot, mind the heath at night. The pale lamps make shadows that move. Some of the shadows are only shadows.
Priest, you will want to see Hester. She was bitten as a girl, and she has opinions about holy light.
Cael hunts the werewolves, not for the bounty but for the mercy of it. He keeps a silver blade, and a sorry heart.
Ivo buries the dead. Lately he has had to bury the wolves too, when the moon lets them rest. He says they look younger, afterwards.
Juniper lights the east posts at dusk. She is nine and refuses help. I let her. A girl should have one job that is entirely her own.
Corvin keeps his telescope on the roof of the old mill. He says the moon here is wrong. I say a moon is only wrong when it stops being kind.
Maud's inn serves honest ale and a very small portion of honest silence. It is the finest bed on the moor.
Tobias sells silver oil at a fair price. He grinds it himself from old coin, and he will not tell me whose.
A merchant of rare things came here once, in daylight, which is impossible. He sold me a candle that burns without wax. It is in the cellar. I do not light it.
The pale lamps feed on dusk. Every evening, the last red of the sky is drawn out of the heath and fed into them. That is why the moor stays dark.
The stone ring lies through the depths, east of the Hold. Take silver oil, and plenty of it. Take a friend who can cast. And do not follow a light you did not light yourself.
The great lamp has gone dark. I watched from the wall: a gap in the night, shrinking. The moor sighed, and the wind turned warm.
Garrow is sitting by my hearth, eating soup. He has not said a word. He has not stopped crying, either. Maybe it is the soup.
The Grave Barrow, past the eastern bend, holds something silver-furred that is neither wolf nor man. Cael says it is a hybrid. Ivo says it is a grave-guard. I say nobody goes near it.
Whatever lay in the barrow now sleeps. I went to the rim of the heath this morning and, for once, the wind brought no howling.
Whatever waits at Keep Vael, remember: you carry a flame of your own. Tend it, and it will outlast any pale flame.

tobias_krane.name: Tobias Krane
tobias_krane.personality: dry, careful, secretly sentimental about his own wares
tobias_krane.voice: weights and wicks, tidy sentences with the corners squared off

say: Tobias Krane, chandler. Lamplight Goods. We sell everything that burns, and a few things that put it out.
Silver oil is the item to buy. A flask coats a blade for six turns, and ghosts, wraiths and the moor's wolves will feel it. I grind it fresh each morning from old coin.

lines.text: A candle burns at the rate of its wick. A lamp burns at the rate of its owner's patience.
Silver oil is two parts moor-poppy, one part ground coin and a pinch of prayer. The prayer is optional. The coin is not.
I have sold forty thousand lamps and one very expensive mirror. The mirror still has not found a buyer. It has too much of an opinion.
A flask coats one weapon for six turns. Buy one per fighter, and one spare for the fight you did not expect.
Long ago we used tallow. It stank, and it smoked. Beeswax is better, and moor-poppy better still. I defend that sentence against all comers.
My shop has eleven shelves, and I know the position of every wick. Move one and I will notice by dawn.
Sword-bearer: silver oil on the blade, and aim for the joints. A wraith will flinch, and a werewolf will hesitate. That is all the advantage you need.
Caster: you will not need the oil. Spend your coin on ether, and keep your mana for the wraiths.
Light-foot: a silvered dagger is the most underrated weapon in the dark. Dip it twice before a patrol.
Priest: my best sellers are phoenix plumes and clear tea. Banshees put people to sleep, and sleepers need waking.
Orsolya buys the cheapest wicks I stock and the dearest oil. She says wicks are expendable and oil is a trust.
Cael visits every week for silver filings. He never asks the price. I never tell him. We are both proud of the arrangement.
Ivo buys black candles for the graves. They burn slowly, and they are not for sale to anybody who is alive.
Hester asked me for a lamp that does not cast a shadow. I told her it does not exist. She said she knew, and bought it anyway.
Juniper buys wicks by the handful, paying in buttons. I accept the buttons. I have a drawer of them. It is my favourite drawer.
Corvin wants a lamp in the shade of moonlight. I have been working on one for eleven years. It comes out blue, or it comes out nothing.
A rare trader's wagon trundled past the shop in daylight once. He did not stop, and he did not buy. Seldom have I been so insulted by a back view.
Pale lamps are never sold. I have tried to examine one. It was cold, and the cold stayed in my fingers for a week.
Silver oil first, ether second, tea third. In that order. Anyone who buys them in a different order learns the order the hard way.
Garrow Thane was my best customer, years ago. He bought a lamp every month, and he always asked for the biggest. I should have wondered what he was lighting.
The big lamp is dark, and my shop is full. People want every kind of light at once. I am not complaining.
Something silver-furred lurks in the barrow, east of the road. If you kill it, I will pay well for a pelt. I would use it for polish. Do not ask what it polishes.
Silvered gear works on wraiths without oil, and on wolves without oil. Good to know, if you still own any.
May your wick be long and your oil clean. It is the oldest wish in the trade, and also the shortest.

maud_ferris.name: Maud Ferris
maud_ferris.role: keeper of the Wick & Wax Inn
maud_ferris.personality: plump, shrewd, soft-spoken, a listener first and a landlady second
maud_ferris.voice: inn-keeper's talk: beds, sheets and who left without paying; very good at the pause that gets a confession

say: Maud Ferris. This is the Wick and Wax. A hundred coins a night, a lamp beside every pillow, and a bowl of porridge that tastes of nothing but is very, very warm.
No guest has ever been refused, even those with claws. The rule is: lamps stay lit, doors stay latched, and nobody sleeps alone in the attic.

lines.text: A good inn has a lamp in every window, and a very small cat in every corner. Mine has eleven of each.
Guests on the moor sleep lightly. I put a pinch of lavender in the pillows. It helps, until the howling starts.
The porridge is oats, water and a little salt. It is a very plain recipe. People who say otherwise have usually been very hungry.
Every bed in the Wick and Wax has a name. Beside the door lies Hope. Up in the attic lies Regret. We try not to let anyone sleep in Regret.
I serve tea in the evening to anyone who looks like they need it, and to a few who do not. Both groups tip, in their way.
The inn has stood for ninety years. It has survived two plagues, a fire and a very long argument between my grandmother and the mayor.
Sword-bearer, An extra blanket lies folded on your bed. You will not use it. But you will know it is there, and sleep better for that.
Caster, there is a basin of water beside your pillow, for any stray spark. The last wizard here set the curtains alight twice in one night.
Light-foot, the little room over the scullery has a window you can open without anyone hearing. I leave it unlatched on the nights I trust the guest.
Priest, there is an old woman in room four who is very sick and very proud. She would take a kind word from you better than from me.
Orsolya sleeps here on the nights the lamps are quiet. She sleeps sitting up, with her scissors in her hand. I do not tell her it is silly.
Cael has a room I keep for him, always. He rarely uses it. He says the bed is too soft for a man who needs to stay awake.
Ivo takes a bowl of porridge at midnight. He never speaks. I think he likes the company of someone who is not grieving.
Hester knits in the corner, and she always makes a scarf too long. I think she is knitting for the person she used to be.
Juniper brings me a handful of lamp-wicks every evening. I use them for the oven. She thinks I use them for the lamps. I do not correct her.
Corvin stares at the stars out of the attic window, even though I have asked him not to. I have given up. I leave a candle by the sill.
A rare trader once left a cup of something silver on my table. I tried a drop. It tasted of a time that never happened. I have not been the same.
When the moon is out, I open the shutters, all of them, and let the room fill with silver. It is the only time the inn is quiet.
Going up to the ring? Sleep first. Eat first. Return and give me the whole tale. That is the whole arrangement, and it is a good one.
Word has come that the great lamp died! A guest ran in from the road to say so. I put the kettle on. I did not even look at the clock.
Garrow Thane is in room six, with a blanket and a bowl. He has not said anything. He keeps touching his own hands, as if to check they are still there.
I hear something silver-furred sleeps in the barrow. I leave it a bowl of porridge on the first of the month. It is always clean in the morning.
Silver oil is for fighting. Hot porridge is for after. Never confuse the two, and never skip the second.
Come back. A bed named Hope waits beside the door, and it has your shape in it already.

cael_redmark.name: Cael Redmark
cael_redmark.personality: lean, grim, sorrowful; the sort of man who apologises to what he kills
cael_redmark.voice: short, flat statements; hunting lore delivered like a funeral reading

lines.text: I hunt what comes down off the moor. I do not enjoy it. I do it carefully, and I do it kindly, and I count each one.
Silver does what steel will not. It does not cut deeper. It cuts truer. A werewolf feels it the way you feel a lie.
Wraiths pass through a blade like smoke. A silvered edge, a flame or a spell will hold them. Pick any of the three, and do not hesitate.
A werewolf that is hurt below half its strength goes wild. It hits harder, it moves faster, and it does not stop. Finish it while it is still thinking.
The pack always has a howler. The howler calls the others. Kill it first, or you will be surrounded in three turns.
I have a silver knife, a silver arrow and a silver bullet that I have never fired. It is for the day I am the one it is meant for.
Sword-bearer, dip the blade in oil before every fight. Do it as you walk, without breaking stride. A pause is a mistake on this moor.
Caster, aim at the howlers. A spell will not stop a wraith, but it will frighten a wolf, and a frightened wolf makes mistakes.
Light-foot, silver your arrows, not your dagger. A bow keeps you out of reach, and out of reach is the only safe distance.
Priest, light is the hunter's oldest ally. A sun-prayer will singe a wraith's cloak and a wolf's temper. Use it freely.
Hester is the only person I know who was bitten and lived. She does not blame the wolf. She does not blame anyone. It unsettles me.
Ivo buries what I leave behind. We have never spoken about it. We have an understanding that we will not.
Juniper asks me every night if I killed a monster. I tell her I only helped a few wolves go home. She seems to understand the difference.
Corvin tracks the moon, and I track the wolves. We both end the month knowing exactly when the worst night will fall.
Orsolya feeds me whether I want it or not. I have stopped arguing. A man cannot fight the woman who keeps his lamp lit.
Maud keeps my room. I have used it six times in nine years. The rest of the nights, I am out there, in the grey, listening.
A rare trader handed me a silver arrow once. He said it would find the right target. I never did learn what he meant. It rides in my quiver, at the back.
Garrow Thane was a friend. I do not say that lightly. He taught me to track. He taught me to count my breaths. Now I am on the moor, and he is under the pale lamp, and which of us got the worse deal.
The depths are crawling with wolves and wraiths. Silver oil, a good party, and the sense to retreat. Garrow will not hold it against you.
The big lamp has gone out. I heard the wolves stop howling. Every one of them together. I stood on the wall and counted. It took a very long time to get to a hundred.
Garrow knows me. He nodded. It was only a small nod, and it was the nicest thing that has happened to me in thirty years.
A hybrid in the barrow, half werewolf and half true wolf. I have seen its tracks. They are the biggest I have ever followed. I have not followed them far.
The barrow is empty of howls. I walked to the mouth of it this morning. There was only wind, and the smell of old fur.
Hunt kindly. Count each one. And when the count gets too high, sit down and have a bowl of Maud's porridge. It is the only cure.

ivo_ashby.name: Ivo Ashby
ivo_ashby.personality: stooped, dry-humoured, quietly comfortable in the company of the dead
ivo_ashby.voice: deadpan, tidy grave-talk: depths, soil, headstones, patience

lines.text: Six feet down is the rule. Seven for the unquiet. Eight for the very unquiet. I have never needed nine.
The moor soil is peat. It keeps what it is given. I have dug up a farmer from three hundred years back with his hat still on.
I give each grave a black candle and a small stone. The stone is for the living. The candle is for the dead. They do not mind sharing.
Wraiths are the dead who forgot how to stop. I bear no hate for them. I only ask that they keep to the moor, and not wander into the village.
Banshees wail when the wind turns. It is a lament, not a threat. It becomes a threat only when you have not heard a lament in years.
Peace is not the absence of noise. It is the presence of enough room to hear the noise without minding.
Sword-bearer, if a wraith comes at you, do not swing. Swing and you will cut air. Light a lamp, or find a silver blade, and say a short prayer.
Caster, the dead listen to spells the way they listen to voices. If you must fight them, be polite, and be brief.
Light-foot, the barrow mound is hollow. Do not crawl in without a rope. The last man who did called it a cave. The cave called him dinner.
Priest, you are welcome to bless any grave you like. They are all unmarked. I would be grateful, and so would they.
I have buried nineteen werewolves in the last month. They look much younger in death. I cannot say why that comforts me.
Cael leaves the bodies by the gate each morning. I have asked him to knock. He says he does not want to wake me. I am awake.
Hester visits my work every Sunday. She sits on the wall and does not talk. I think she is practising.
Juniper asked me if the dead are afraid of the dark. I told her no, they are only afraid of being forgotten. She gave me a candle.
Corvin says the moon is closer than it should be. I say the dead have noticed, and they are restless about it.
Orsolya carries me soup whenever I look underfed. I have always eaten. I take it anyway, out of courtesy.
A rare trader tried selling me an hourglass that runs backward. I said I only deal with things that stay put. He left, laughing.
Garrow Thane's wife is buried here. I tend her grave every week. He does not know. I think he would like to.
The depths predate the village itself. If you find a grave without a marker, do not step on it. It will be somebody's grandmother.
The great lamp died, and the graves are quiet. I put down my shovel and stood in the dark for a moment. It was very good.
Garrow came to his wife's grave this morning. He did not say anything. He knelt, and I left the lamp, and I went away.
The barrow is a very old grave. Whatever rests there was a guard once, and then a beast, and now it is something between. I leave the mound alone.
The barrow is open, they say. I will go and fill it in. A grave should be shut, and respectfully.
I have a spare shovel, and a very patient way with questions. Return when the road wears you down, and I will say what the moor remembers.

hester_blight.name: Hester Blight
hester_blight.role: village elder, bitten as a girl
hester_blight.personality: gentle, grey, endlessly forgiving, with a flicker of steel when pressed
hester_blight.voice: knitting-needle rhythm, memories told in the present tense, a way of making cruelty sound like weather

lines.text: I was bitten at nine, on a night like this. I am eighty-one now. I outlived the cure, the cursed and most of my kin.
It is not the pain, dear. It is the waiting. Every month you wonder if this is the night the moon calls your name.
The wolf that bit me was a boy. He had a toy horse in his pocket. It has sat in my drawer seventy-two years. There is nobody to return it to.
I hold no grudge. A grudge is a very heavy thing to knit, and I have enough scarves.
The pale lamp turned the quiet ones loud. Those who had slept for generations woke hungry. That is a cruel trick, to wake someone to hunger.
A werewolf does not choose. That is all of it. Hold on to that when you meet one, even when you must strike.
Sword-bearer, silver does not heal what it harms. It only makes the harm honest. Use it gently.
Caster, I once met a mage who cured a bite with a spell. It did not take. It left the wolf, but it took the girl. Be careful what you cure.
Light-foot, the moor is full of paths that only the bitten know. I could sketch you a map. It would be very short. It would end at the stones.
Priest, I have prayed every night for seventy years. The sun may not hear. But I know I am heard, and that is enough.
Cael hunts my kin, and he does it kindly. I make him a scarf every winter. He wears it under his armour and does not tell anyone.
Ivo digs the graves. I sit with him. We do not speak. It is a very restful form of company.
Juniper brings me a lamp every evening. She sets it on the sill, and she looks at my face, and she is not afraid. It is a rare and wonderful thing.
Corvin tells me when the full moon is coming. I make tea, and I lock the door, and we both pretend it is a tea party.
Orsolya let me stay in the Hold when everyone else would not. I owe her every winter, every blanket and every candle.
Tobias sells me silver thread. I knit it into my scarves. It hurts. It is a small penance, and I like it.
A rare trader pressed a ball of yarn on me that never ran out. I knit for a year before I realised it was getting longer. I have a scarf now that reaches the inn.
Garrow Thane lost his wife to the same moon that took my youth. We used to sit together on the wall. I would give a great deal to sit with him again.
He will not know you. He will not know himself. But somewhere, under the claws, there is a man who used to love bread and brass. Be kind to him.
I felt the moon change. It did not hurt, which has not happened in seventy years. I sat on the wall and let it shine on my face.
Garrow sat with me this evening. We did not speak. He took the end of my scarf and held it. No finer conversation have I had.
The creature in the barrow is my brother's grandson, I think. He was lost on the moor in my girlhood. If you find him, tell him the porridge is on.
He is at rest, then. I put the toy horse on his grave, in my mind. It seemed the proper place for it.
Walk gently, dear. Darkness is only a kind of quiet. It is the things we bring into it that make it loud.

juniper_cole.name: Juniper Cole
juniper_cole.personality: fierce, tiny, dead serious about her one job
juniper_cole.voice: clipped, businesslike; speaks about lamps as if they were soldiers under her command

lines.text: I am Juniper. I light the east posts. All forty-one. In order. Do not talk to me while I am working. I will lose count.
You take the pole, you touch the wick, you count to three. If the flame is yellow, you go on. If it is blue, you run.
Blue flame means the pale lamps are near. Orsolya says it is nothing. I say it is a very small and very serious something.
I am the best lamplighter in the Hold. Orsolya says so. She also says I should eat. I say I will, after the east posts.
The moon is a lamp that somebody forgot to trim. That is what my grandfather said. I think he was right.
The pale lamps displease me. They are cold. A lamp is supposed to be warm. That is what it is for.
Sword-bearer, do you have a sword that glows? A real one? Show me one. I would hold the lamp for you.
Caster, can you light a lamp without a pole? I am curious. I have been practising with a very long match.
Light-foot, if you hear something behind you on the moor, do not look back. Look at your lamp. It is always right.
Priest, have you lit a lamp for someone who is gone? I do. It is the one on the far east post. It is very bright.
Cael says wolves are merely hungry, never monsters. I told him a hungry thing should be given soup. He did not know what to say.
Ivo lets me light the candles on the graves. I light them very gently. I think the dead like it.
Hester gave me a scarf. It is too long. I wear it twice round, and it still drags on the ground. I own nothing finer.
Corvin lets me look through his telescope. The moon has a face. It looks tired. I told it to go to bed. I doubt it listened.
Tobias sells me wicks for buttons. I have two hundred buttons. They are all different. I have never run out.
Maud puts extra porridge in my bowl. I eat all of it. It is my second favourite thing after lamps.
A man with a painted wagon gave me a candle that does not burn down. It lives in my pocket. I light it when I am scared. It is the best candle in the world.
One day I will be the Lamp-Mother. Orsolya says I have to learn to share. I say I will share. After I light them all.
You are going up to the stones? Take a lamp. A real one, a yellow one. The pale ones are no good at all, and here is the reason. They are lonely.
The big lamp went out! I saw it! The whole sky went dark and then the moon came out, and it was lovely! I forgot to count the east posts!
I lit all forty-one posts and the moon is still out! Do you think they will leave it on? I hope they leave it on!
Hester says there is a wolf in the barrow who is her cousin. A wolf cannot be a cousin, surely. But I would give it soup, anyway.
The barrow is hushed. I put a candle by it. A yellow one, so it knows the way home.
You can borrow my candle, if you want. It never burns down. I will want it back. But you can borrow it for a while.

corvin_black.name: Corvin Black
corvin_black.personality: gaunt, sleepless, tender about the sky and awkward about everything else
corvin_black.voice: star-names, angle-measures, and a habit of stopping mid-sentence to look up

lines.text: The moon over Hollowmoor is wrong. It hangs nearer than it ought to, and thinner. It hangs there as if it were being pulled.
My log holds every night. Eleven thousand entries. The last forty repeat one line: the dusk is not coming.
The pale lamps drain the evening. Every night the red goes out of the west a little earlier, and the heath goes dark a little sooner.
A real dusk has seven colours. I have seen only three in the last two months. I miss the other four very much.
I used to be a scholar in the Silverhush library. I left because the stars were louder than the books.
The Chancellor passed through here with a wagon draped in black. Every lamp in the Hold flickered as it went by. I wrote down the time: seventeen past dusk, at the third post.
Sword-bearer, silver and moonlight are cousins. A silvered blade in the moon's light will cut a little deeper. I have measured it. It is not a lot.
Caster, the moon's pull is strongest on spells of the tide and the shadow. Light spells fare better. Do not ask me for the equations.
Light-foot, you could use the stars to cross the heath. I could draw you a chart. It would be a poor chart. The stars are not behaving.
Priest, I would be grateful for a blessing on my telescope. It cracked in the cold. I doubt it will help, but I would feel better.
Orsolya brings me tea at dawn, when I fall asleep over the log. I always wake with a blanket. I never see who put it there.
Cael hunts at the full moon. I tell him the date. He thanks me. I think he is the only person who reads my log.
Ivo asked me once if the dead can see the stars. I said I did not know. He said he hoped so. It is a good hope.
Hester says the moon is the oldest wolf in the sky. She says it howls once a month, and nobody hears. I like that.
Juniper asks to look through my telescope every evening. She has named the moon. She calls it Tired. I have written it in the log.
Tobias is trying to make a lamp tinted like the moon. I told him the moon has no single colour. He claimed that was the point.
A rare trader hawked me a star in a jar. The whole jar was beyond my purse. He gave me a fragment, free. It is in a drawer, humming.
My theory is that the sun is not dying. I think it is hiding. That the pale lamps are not drinking the dusk, but keeping it from something. I cannot prove it.
The stone ring on the hill was built to watch the moon. The big lamp stands where the old altar was. Break the lamp, and the ring will remember what it was for.
The great lamp died! I looked up and the moon was the right size, and the right colour, and the right distance. I wrote it down, and then I wept on the log.
The dusk is back. Seven colours, in order, with a very thin line of green at the end. I intend to write about it until Sunday.
A thing lives in the Grave Barrow. On full-moon nights, it howls in a pattern. I have charted it. It is a lullaby, I think. A very old one.
The barrow is silent on the full moon. I sat up all night to be sure. It was the quietest night of my life, and I cried a little.
Whatever you find at Keep Vael, look up. At night, from the black cliffs, the sky is very clear. You will see the shape of the thing the Chancellor is building.
